newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia PM says may amend Aboriginal land laws.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM says may amend Aboriginal land laws.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Tuesday a court ruling that Aboriginal land claims could co-exist with so-called "pastoral leases" could prompt the government to amend laws on indigenous land rights.

In a move that dismayed rural politicians and farmers, Australia's High Court ruled on Monday that pastoral leases -- land leased to farmers or cattlemen -- did not automatically override claims by Aborigines.

"I am disappointed that yesterday's High Court decision in the Wik case failed to clarify satisfactorily uncertainties concerning the effect of native title on pastoral leases," Howard said in a statement.

The High Court, Australia's highest court of appeal, decided to uphold an appeal by the Aboriginal Wik people against an earlier decision denying them the right to lodge a native title claim to more than 35,000 sq kms (13,500 sq miles) of land in the far north state of Queensland.
Monday's ruling means as much as 40 percent of Australia's vast territory could become the subject of complex legal action.

Farmers and mining companies, whose mines are often situated on pastoral leases, had hoped the High Court would move to clarify native title issues, clouded by uncertainty since the introduction of native title legislation in 1993.
But Howard said the ruling created more confusion since it threatened the assumption, on which the 1993 laws were based, that pastoral leases took priority over native title claims.
"The judgement therefore has obvious ramifications for the Native Title Act as currently framed," Howard said.
"It raises questions well beyond those which the government's current amendments were proposed to address."
The government has introduced into parliament amendments that would make it more difficult for Aboriginal groups to force negotiations on land claims.

"The government will urgently consult with state and territory governments and other interested parties about whether the Native Title Act needs to be further amended in light of yesterday's judgement," Howard said.
The amendments are due to be debated in parliament early next year.

Australian farmers warned on Monday that the ruling could lead to a rash of new native title claims. The chief minister of the outback Northern Territory said 96 percent of the 1.34 million sq kms (520,000 sq miles) of the Territory was now vulnerable to Aboriginal claims.

In 1992, the High Court overturned the historical idea of Terra Nullius -- that Australia was an empty land when white settlers arrived in 1788 -- thus recognising that Aborigines had traditional land rights.
In 1993, the Labor government passed legislation allowing Aborigines to claim land if they could prove uninterrupted traditional use of that land.
